name: Carla Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal day on a building site for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three, and I lead a crew measuring and fixing roof timbers on building sites. I have a trade certificate and people call me when the drawing and the wall plate disagree. I use an AI tool now and then to compare a materials list, after checking what the other leads have found useful. My partner and I have two children at school, a mortgage and a few months of expenses saved; my pay is about usual for the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the roof crew to take the small time saving and keep measuring. An AI materials list does not carry a roof timber safely across a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would expect my job and wage to be steady. Our savings cover a few months, and there are some similar jobs nearby, so I would not change course over a tidier list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting out the roof and checking the timber lengths with my crew. I would use the list tool occasionally when another lead has shown it works, then mark any mismatch by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work in this picture. A quicker list is useful if it leaves our paid fitting days intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which measurement would you never take from a list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The span between the actual wall plates. I check it on site before any timber is cut, because the built walls can differ from the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you increase savings just for this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We already have a few months set aside, and the job looks stable here. I would not call existing money a new saving decision.

say: I would **take** small ordering gains while keeping physical roof measurements.
I would **only** use the list tool where another lead has shown it works.
think: My **roof** work and usual wage look steady in this picture.
A **few** months of savings and some nearby jobs let me judge the tool calmly.
do: **Keep** leading roof setting-out and checking actual wall-plate spans.
**Use** familiar AI materials list only after a proven site check.
S0.quote: An AI materials list does not carry a roof timber safely across a building site.
fieldNote: **Carla** uses AI occasionally for lists and checks its numbers against physical roof spans.
**Typical** pay, moderate savings and some nearby jobs support calm when AI makes only a small difference.

steps.text: Keep leading and measuring building-site roof work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster buying and planning might help our roof jobs if deliveries arrive on time. I would test a new AI schedule only after a neighbouring crew has used it without losing paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry a clever schedule could give management a reason to squeeze our fitting days. My partner and I could cover a short gap, but the mortgage would still need a regular wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the roof crew and compare the new schedule with actual delivery dates on two jobs. If those results hold, I would learn its controls; I would also ask the manager for written paid-hour terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut in paid days, though I can test the schedule and speak up. The roof itself still needs carpenters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a good test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Timber arrives when the crew is paid to fit it, and our measured spans match the order. A roof schedule is only faster if the timber arrives while my crew is being paid to fit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you ask about the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead on the next site how the schedule treated their crew. I trust a finished roof and the pay record more than a sales screen.

say: I would **test** a proven AI schedule against real roof deliveries and paid hours.
I would **ask** management to show the crew’s hours and rate in writing.
think: Our **mortgage** could feel a shorter fitting week despite some savings.
I **am** willing to learn controls after seeing another crew’s result.
do: **Compare** AI schedule with actual roof deliveries on two jobs.
**Learn** new scheduling controls if site test preserves paid time.
**Ask** manager for written roof-crew hours and wage terms.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-day loss, with practical tests available.
S1.quote: A roof schedule is only faster if the timber arrives while my crew is being paid to fit it.
fieldNote: She is **open** to learning a new tool after another crew and her own delivery records prove it.
**Potential** lost paid fitting days justify anxiety even though she has a moderate cushion.

steps.text: Keep paid roof shifts while checking terms
Learn new AI scheduling controls after paid-hour test

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that thinking AI can redraw roofs in 2028 when I am forty-five, but capable hands-on robots come around 2031 when I am forty-eight. The first date changes plans; the second could change how many carpenters fit them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think routine roof assembly might lose paid hours once robots arrive, while awkward repairs could still need us. A few months saved and some nearby jobs help, but I cannot promise another lead vacancy will open exactly then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the roof work and record the difficult corrections we make so the builder can see the skilled part. If 2031 robots reduce my paid hours, I would apply to actual local repair-lead vacancies only if the wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about an uncertain cut, not certain of a complete loss. I have time to gather proof and some money to search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the correction record contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A photograph of the wall plate, the measured span and the timber we changed. I would keep the record with the job paperwork, not pretend it is a new AI skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for a repair role before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a posted nearby role with clear pay that covers the household. A robot may fit the standard roof in 2031, but the mortgage is due on the crooked one too.

say: **Thinking** AI changes roof plans in 2028; capable building robots follow around 2031.
I would **keep** measured examples of repairs that a standard roof plan misses.
think: **Robot** fitting may cut routine paid hours, but the size of the loss is unknown.
**Savings** and some local jobs permit a search if a real adequate vacancy appears.
do: **Record** measured corrections to awkward roof jobs while staying employed.
**Apply** after paid-hour cuts to posted local repair-lead job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible routine-hour losses, with a search cushion.
S2.quote: A robot may fit the standard roof in 2031, but the mortgage is due on the crooked one too.
fieldNote: She does **not** confuse documenting existing carpentry judgment with learning a new AI tool.
Her **possible** move depends on actual lost paid hours and a posted nearby role with adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep roof work and document measured corrections
Apply for posted local repair-lead role with household-covering pay after hour cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that 2031 thinking AI reaches me at forty-eight, with hands-on robots about 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five years is enough to see whether robot-built roofs need a paid site checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider training for roof inspection if the course is funded, the study time is paid and there is a posted local job I could actually take. A roof inspection course is an investment only when the study days and the eventual local job both pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the roof crew and ask a builder about funded paid-time inspection training. I would enroll only once those terms and a suitable posted local role are clear; after qualifying, I would apply only if its wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the future and anxious if the builder plans fewer fitting hours. Having real course and job terms would settle some of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does inspection add to your roof experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Formal checks for fixings and a signed record, rather than just correcting our own crew’s work. I would need the certificate before seeking that responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is paid but no local vacancy is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my current paid crew and wait to enroll. A certificate is useful only if a real job at a suitable wage exists nearby.

say: The 2031 **planning** change gives time before robots reach roof fitting around 2034.
I would **study** inspection only with funded paid time and a posted local role.
think: My **roof** skill could transfer, but formal inspection needs a credential.
I would **not** spend wages on training or accept a role below household costs.
do: **Keep** leading paid roof work while checking actual inspection openings.
**Enroll** in funded roof inspection course only with paid time and posted suitable local role.
**Apply** after qualification only to posted local inspector job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** if hours shrink, with a conditional route over five years.
S3.quote: A roof inspection course is an investment only when the study days and the eventual local job both pay.
fieldNote: Her **steady** adaptability supports formal training when proof, funding, paid time and job terms align.
The **enquiry** itself is not training; enrollment follows an actual posted local opportunity.

steps.text: Keep paid roof shifts while checking openings
Enroll in funded paid-time inspection course for posted suitable local role
Apply after qualification to posted local inspector job with adequate pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew I will be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots fit roofs around 2039. A decade gives me time to build savings from wages and watch what the first site robots actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stay in skilled roof work for quite a while if the builder keeps paying for careful fitting. I would not count on being an inspector without a funded course on paid time and a posted role nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading roofs and add a new amount from each paid month to our reserve after mortgage and school bills. If a funded, paid-time roof inspection course and posted local role at adequate wages appear, I would enroll and then apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about later machines, but the next years look manageable. A decade before roof robots is enough time to save wages, not a reason to spend our existing cushion on guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tells you the reserve is really growing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark the actual transfer from each paid month, after the usual bills clear. The months already saved are a cushion, not a fresh contribution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an inspection offer in another region?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look first at posted local jobs because the children are in school and we have a mortgage. A distant suggestion without a wage figure is not a plan.

say: A **decade** gives me time to add new wages to savings and watch real roof robots.
I would **keep** physical carpentry unless funded paid training and a suitable local role justify a move.
think: The **household** is fairly secure now, but a mortgage rewards steady new saving.
An **inspection** title without a posted job and adequate pay is not security.
do: **Save** new amounts from paid roof wages after mortgage and school bills.
**Keep** leading roof work while monitoring actual robot use.
**Enroll** in funded paid-time inspection course for posted adequate local role.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current work remains fairly secure.
S4.quote: A decade before roof robots is enough time to save wages, not a reason to spend our existing cushion on guesses.
fieldNote: Her **plan** adds genuinely new savings from wages and retains paid carpentry work.
She would **train** only with funding, paid time, a posted nearby role and pay that covers the household.

steps.text: Save new money from paid roof wages after bills
Keep paid roof fitting while monitoring site robots
Enroll in funded paid-time inspection course for posted adequate local job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028/2031 picture worries me most because routine roof hours might shrink. A builder willing to show paid-hour plans and an actual local repair or inspection opening at a mortgage-covering wage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a course has paid study days. I can use a new tool after it proves itself, but I will not spend our mortgage reserve chasing a job that has not been posted. A sound roof starts with the span I measured, not the tidy line an AI drew.

headlineQuote: A sound roof starts with the span I measured, not the tidy line an AI drew.
portrait: **Carla** is a forty-three-year-old trade-certified lead carpenter who sets out building-site roofs.
Her **typical** pay, mortgage, two schoolchildren and one to six months saved shape a measured approach.
She **uses** AI occasionally and learns new controls after they prove useful on real jobs.
She **considers** repair or inspection work only with paid training, a posted local role and household-covering wages.
biggestWorry: The **fast** 2028/2031 case could reduce routine paid roof-fitting hours after capable robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** paid-hour plans and a posted nearby repair or inspection job with a mortgage-covering wage would help.
